title: A positive multiple of a fundamental character extends from the big cell
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $H$ be a reductive $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme], meaning smooth, connected, affine and of finite type, with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. Unipotent means unipotent matrices in a faithful representation at geometric points. Fix a split maximal torus $T_H$, a Borel subgroup $B_H$, unipotent radical $U_H$, projection $p_H:B_H\to T_H$, and roots and coroots as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Assume moreover that $H$ is semisimple and simply connected, meaning that it has no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup and every surjective homomorphism to $H$ from a semisimple group with finite central kernel is an isomorphism. Solvable means that successive commutator subgroup schemes become trivial; finite means finite-dimensional coordinate algebra and central means commuting after every scalar extension. Let $\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_r$ be its fundamental characters, characterized by $\langle\omega_i,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle=\delta_{ij}$ as in [lem-sfb-simply-connected-character-lattice]. Write $w_0$ for the Weyl group element reversing the positive roots, choose a representative $n_0\in N_H(T_H)(F)$, and put $C=U_Hn_0B_H$. Here $N_H(T_H)$ is the subgroup normalizing $T_H$, the Weyl group is $N_H(T_H)(F)/T_H(F)$, and $(w\chi)(t)=\chi(n^{-1}tn)$. For every $1\le i\le r$ there exist an integer $d_i>0$ and $h_i\in F[H]$ whose restriction to $C$ is
$$h_i(u n_0 b)=\bigl((w_0\omega_i)(p_H(b))\bigr)^{-d_i}.$$
The formula is an identity of regular functions, equivalently it holds after every commutative $F$-algebra extension. No characteristic restriction is imposed.

source.place: Lemma 22.24 and proof, printed p.469, followed by the first three sentences of the proof of Lemma 22.25 (the regular function for a positive multiple). Definition 22.21 and Proposition 22.22 fix the normalization on U n_0 B.

proof.text: Fix $i$; if $r=0$ there is nothing to prove. The parabolic input supplies $B_H\subseteq P_i\ne H$. Chevalley's theorem gives a finite-dimensional rational representation $V$ and a line $L=Fv$ whose stabilizer on every $F$-algebra is exactly $P_i$. The action on $L$ is a group-scheme character of $P_i$. Its restriction to $U_H$ is trivial by the unipotent-to-multiplicative input. Thus, writing $\lambda$ for its restriction to $T_H$, the identity $B_H=U_H\rtimes T_H$ gives $bv=\lambda(p_H(b))v$ after every scalar extension. Replace $V$ by the smallest rational submodule $M$ containing $v$. Such a submodule exists by intersecting the submodules containing $v$; tensoring vector spaces over $F$ preserves these intersections inside the finite-dimensional $V$. The line has the same stabilizer in $M$ as in $V$, since $M\otimes_F A\hookrightarrow V\otimes_F A$ for every $A$.

source.place: Theorem 12.12, pp.234--235; Proposition 22.17 and Lemma 22.15, pp.466--467.

proof.text: Write $\lambda=\sum_j d_j\omega_j$, with $d_j\in\mathbf Z$, using the simply connected character lattice. For $j\ne i$, the rank-one reflection input gives an element of $W$ acting by $x\mapsto x-\langle x,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle\alpha_j$ and permuting $\Phi$; it agrees with $s_j$ on $X\otimes\mathbf Q$, which the simple roots span: the composite of the two reflections permutes the finite spanning set $\Phi$, so has finite order, and is unipotent, fixing $\alpha_j$ and acting trivially modulo $\mathbf Q\alpha_j$. Choose a representative $n_j\in N_H(T_H)(F)$. It belongs to $P_i(F)$, so preserves $Fv$; it need not fix $v$ pointwise. By the preceding weight calculation its nonzero image of $v$ has weight both $\lambda$ and $s_j\lambda$. Hence $s_j\lambda=\lambda$. The reflection formula then gives $d_j\alpha_j=0$, so $d_j=0$ since the simple roots form a rational basis. Thus $\lambda=d\omega_i$ for an integer $d$. The weight $s_i\lambda$ occurs and is at most $\lambda$, so $d\alpha_i=\lambda-s_i\lambda\in Q_+$. Linear independence of the simple roots implies $d\geq0$.

proof.text:
Put $\mu=w_0\lambda$. This is the least weight of $M$: for any weight $
u$, the weight $w_0
u$ satisfies $\lambda-w_0
u\in Q_+$, and applying $w_0$ gives $
u-\mu\in Q_+$. Here $w_0(Q_+)=-Q_+$ because $w_0^2=1$ and $w_0\Phi^+=-\Phi^+$. The vector $z=n_0^{-1}v$ has weight $w_0^{-1}\lambda=\mu$. Normalizer conjugation identifies its weight space with $M_\lambda=Fv$, so $M_\mu=Fz$. Define the linear functional $\ell:M	o F$ by $\ell(z)=1$ and by zero on every other weight space. In particular, for every $A$ and $t\in T_H(A)$, $\ell_A(ty)=\mu(t)\ell_A(y)$.

source.place: Lemma 22.15, p.466, and the matrix-coefficient passage in the proof of Lemma 22.25, p.469; lowest-weight calculation expanded.

proof.text:
We check explicitly that $\ell$ is $U_H$-invariant. For a positive root $\alpha$, choose the cited parametrization $u_\alpha:\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\sim}U_\alpha$. If $y\in M_
u$, regularity gives a finite polynomial $u_\alpha(a)y=\sum_{m\geq0}a^m y_m$ with $y_0=y$. Compare coefficients of the universal variable $a$ in $t u_\alpha(a)y=u_\alpha(\alpha(t)a)ty$, using the conjugation identity of the parametrization. It gives $t y_m=
u(t)\alpha(t)^m y_m$, so $y_m\in M_{
u+m\alpha}$. Every weight $
u$ is at least $\mu$. Consequently a term with $m>0$ cannot have weight $\mu$, since $\alpha\in Q_+\setminus\{0\}$ and the simple roots are independent. Applying $\ell$ therefore gives $\ell_A(u_\alpha(a)y)=\ell_A(y)$ for all $A$, first on each weight space and then by linearity. The positive-root product isomorphism expresses every $u\in U_H(A)$ as a product of these root elements. Thus $\ell_A(uy)=\ell_A(y)$ for every $A,u,y$. This polynomial coefficient argument uses torus characters throughout, including in positive characteristic.

source.place: Proposition 22.14 and its coefficient comparison, p.466; Theorem 21.68(a), p.445; the matrix coefficient in Lemma 22.25, p.469, made explicit.

proof.text:
Since $B_H=U_H\rtimes T_H$, the preceding identities imply $\ell_A(by)=\mu(p_H(b))\ell_A(y)$ for all $A,b,y$. Define $h_i(g)=\ell(g^{-1}v)$. This is in $F[H]$: inversion and the representation are morphisms, and $\ell$ is linear. For $u\in U_H(A)$ and $b\in B_H(A)$, the Borel eigenvector identity gives $u^{-1}v=v$, and hence
$$h_i(u n_0 b)=\ell_A(b^{-1}n_0^{-1}u^{-1}v)=\mu(p_H(b))^{-1}\ell_A(z)=\bigl((w_0\omega_i)(p_H(b))\bigr)^{-d_i}.$$
These calculations hold on every commutative $F$-algebra, so they give equality of regular functions on $U_H\times_F B_H$. By the open-immersion chart this is precisely the required restriction to $C$. The normalization $\ell(z)=1$ accommodates the prescribed representative $n_0$; there is no extraction of a $d_i$-th root and no division by $d_i$.

The suppressed d_i>0 inference is expanded correctly (step 4: Q+∩−Q+=0 gives M=Fv, so the stabilizer would be all of H, contradicting P_i≠H). Steps 5-7 build an explicit lowest-weight coefficient ℓ(g^{-1}v), U-invariant by polynomial coefficient comparison on every A, and its value on u n0 b has the right sign and inverse. The new node is exactly Milne 21.88 and is true: rank 0 is vacuous, rank 1 gives P=B, and I also checked SL3 and SL2×SL2. It is a statement only (B1), self-contained and not a restated clause of the item. It is not a duplicate: regular-cocharacter-borel-description covers only regular cocharacters, and rank-one-reflections, Bruhat-cells and rho-orbit give no intermediate subgroups. FIX (C1/C4): step 3 used a representative n_j of s_j∈W, but no cited node puts s_j in W. Borel-pair gives only the automorphism of X, Bruhat-charts gives representatives only for elements already in W, and the new node is vacuous without that. I added lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections to step 3 and proof_deps, with a three-line identification of its reflection with the borel-pair s_j on X_Q, the span of Δ (the composite is unipotent and of finite order, so it is the identity). I also added borel-pair-structure to the uses of steps 4 and 5, for Φ+⊆Q+.
